newsitem.title: USA: Despite cold, U.S. inauguration goes on as planned.
newsitem.headline: Despite cold, U.S. inauguration goes on as planned.

text.p: Despite a blast of bitter Arctic cold, President Bill Clinton's inauguration is expected to be held outdoors as planned on Monday, as are celebrations over the weekend, officials said on Friday.

There are contingency plans if it is forbiddingly cold, like in 1985 when former President Ronald Reagan's swearing-in was moved inside, but officials said the weather should permit the elaborate outdoor ceremony on the steps of the Capitol.

"I'd be real surprised if they didn't hold this thing out front and I'd also be really surprised if they didn't go ahead with the parade," said one congressional official who asked not to be named. "The weather foreast has improved markedly."
Washington was on Friday gripped by unusual cold, with the temperature expected to hit a high of only 20 degrees (minus 6 Celsius). But inaugural officials said it is expected to warm up by Monday.

Eric Ruff, a spokesman for the Joint Inaugural Committee, said that if the weather were to turn colder, a decision would be made on Sunday on whether to move the ceremony inside the Rotunda, the vaulted hall at the centre of the Capitol.
He said this would be at the president's discretion.

If the swearing-in were moved inside, Ruff said only about 1,000 people would be able to attend, including the 535 members of Congress, the Supreme Court and the incoming and outgoing members of the Cabinet.
A weekend celebration with concerts, a musical, food and speeches is expected to go ahead as planned in huge, heated tents on the Mall in central Washington, said inaugural official David Seldin.
"Everything is going forward," he said. "Obviously, people have been aware all along that it's January in Washington and it can be cold out. People have been advised to dress warmly."
